rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the boastful claims are so absurd and arrogant that they receive no answer; the response instead strikes at their arrogance.
rows.anchor: no response is given to them; instead, a fierce blow is dealt to their arrogance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Polytheism is the greatest injustice because it usurps God's greatest right and disgraces the person who commits it.
rows.anchor: By being incriminated with polytheism, a person usurps the greatest right of God and also commits the greatest disgraceful act against his own self.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing a fabricated claim to God is falsehood because people invent it themselves and have no proof for it.
rows.anchor: a person concocts it himself and then ascribes it to God even though he has no argument in its favour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders claimed they too received revelation and could produce a book, seeking to blunt the Prophet's influence; 8:31 cites a parallel boast.
rows.anchor: some leaders of the Quraysh would say that the revelation that the Prophet (sws) claims to receive is also received by them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When truth exposes the arrogant, they use imposing boasts to preserve the deceived public's confidence, but ultimately must concede defeat.
rows.anchor: Then through such imposing statements they try to secure their position so that the common masses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional about seeing the unjust at death has no stated answer because words cannot convey the horrific scene.
rows.anchor: the answer to the condition found in these words is suppressed. This is because words fail to portray the horrific scene

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charge of fabricating falsehood about God refers to the leaders' assertion that they too received divine revelation.
rows.anchor: The words “you would fabricate falsehood about God” refer to their statement that they too received divine revelation from Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ʿan shows that the term for arrogance includes evading God's Book; Islahi identifies arrogant evasion as the most abominable form and a legacy of Satan.
rows.anchor: encompasses the meaning of evasion. There can be many reasons for evading the Book of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh leaders resented honor going to someone outside their ranks and argued that God would have chosen a chief of Makkah or Ṭā’if.
rows.anchor: It is a distinct legacy of Satan. It laid down very heavily on the leaders of the Quraysh that some honour or favour be bestowed to someone outside of them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section ending at 6:94 concludes its monotheism discussion; the next section argues for monotheism from the world around us, also supporting prophethood and the hereafter, and recalls Abraham's method of reflection.
rows.anchor: The above section of verses concluded on the topic of monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across the sūra, monotheism, the hereafter, and prophethood recur; objections and audience responses prompt refutation, explanation, assurance, or directives while the central thread remains intact.
rows.anchor: the content of the sūrah progresses in this same way: central theme, monotheism, hereafter and prophethood are repeatedly discussed in different styles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address becomes direct, as if Judgment Day has arrived, making the terrifying fate described earlier vivid before the audience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They come before God alone, without the wealth, supporters, or intercessors they expected to accompany them.
rows.anchor: They will become before God without any wealth or supporters or intercessors which they thought would be there to help them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans begin without abilities; God develops them and grants resources to test gratitude or arrogance, then they return empty-handed, taking none of it along.
rows.anchor: The purpose is to see whether he becomes grateful to God or shows arrogance. Then comes a day when he returns to God empty handed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject of “the ties between you have been cut” is suppressed; the implied subject is the cord, referring to the absent intercessors.
rows.anchor: the fā‘il in them has been suppressed. The actual construction is to the effect:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's law applies equally to every nation: after a messenger comes, a people must accept reform or face destruction.
rows.anchor: When God sends a messenger to a nation, it is faced with either of the two options: to accept reformation or be put to death.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs knew these nations' stories through vague traditions, especially lacking their moral lessons; the Qur’an restores that history and tells Quraysh to learn that these are their own warning stories.
rows.anchor: Their moral aspect, in particular, was totally ambiguous. The Qur’ ān has lifted the veil from this ambiguity and revived their history.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning to Quraysh begins with accounts of peoples known across Arabia's north, south, and northwest.
rows.anchor: those nations are taken up which became famous while inhabiting the north, the south and the north west of Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nations in these accounts were destroyed for denying their messengers.
rows.anchor: All of them were destroyed because they denied their respective messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accounts follow historical order, so Noah's nation is treated first.
rows.anchor: The sequence adopted is historical. For this reason, the nation of Noah (sws) is taken up the first.
